metadata.title: Consent to Publish Is Not Consent to Be Scored
metadata.topic: GDPR AND READER-TRIGGERED AI AUTHORSHIP SCORING
metadata.purpose: Two independently written legal memos read the same GDPR doctrine against the same feature — Substack's reader-triggered Pangram AI scan — and reach different answers. The film's subject is that disagreement, not the conclusion. Memo A argues from Substack's actual implementation; Memo B argues from architecture in the abstract and never engages the facts. The film sides with neither verdict and instead isolates the three questions no court has answered: whether Pangram is a processor or a joint controller, whether SCHUFA's 'draws strongly' standard survives the jump from one bank to millions of readers, and whether observed redistribution of scores defeats the 'requester-only' mitigation. It closes on the one claim that is close to a clean win regardless — the Article 26 joint-controller gap — and on the strongest argument neither memo made: the EU's own AI Act asks LESS of a human-reviewed writer than Pangram does. Companion piece to 'A P-Value Is Not a Verdict', which handles the statistics; this one handles the law.
metadata.source: Combined GDPR analysis memo (Memo A + Memo B), supplied. Every case citation, date, and platform fact independently verified against primary sources — see FACTCHECK.md. Two claims in the source document were corrected before scripting: the per-post opt-out date, and the scope limit on AI Act Art. 50(4).
metadata.legal_disclaimer: Not legal advice. Stated on screen at B00 and in the description.
